paras: The Dothan buggy attack was an assault by a white mob on a few Black men who were out riding in a buggy in Dothan, Alabama, on a Sunday in the autumn of 1903. The attackers broke down the buggy and drew pistols on the men, and the incident is known only from a Dothan correspondent's letter to the Colored American, which set it among several acts of violence against the town's Black residents.

The letter, printed on 14 November 1903 under the headline "In Darkest Alabama," was written to "call attention" to the treatment of Black people in Dothan. Its writer reported that a Black man had been found "a few days ago" shot to death and hanging from a tree, and that local officers had made no effort to learn who killed him. The writer also described a white groceryman beating a Black woman who asked after an undelivered order, a white crowd that shot into Black homes, and an attack on Black people at the A. M. E. Church "a few weeks ago."

According to the correspondent, "a few colored men" were out riding "a few Sundays ago" when "a mob of whites" attacked them. The attackers broke down the men's buggy, drew pistols on them, and "dared them to speak about it." The letter names neither the men nor their attackers and reports no injuries.

No report of an arrest or prosecution for the attack appears in the coverage. The correspondent closed the account of the town's violence by writing, "I will be glad to see the time come when some action will be taken against this mob violence."

The attack reached print only through the Colored American, which ran the Dothan letter as a "Special" under the headline "In Darkest Alabama." The letter presented the buggy attack as one instance of a pattern of "mob violence" that local officers did not check, rather than as an isolated event. No account of the attack, the hanging, or the church attack was found in the white press.
